Area · Core processes

Thinking

Reasoning, problem solving, decision-making, beliefs and the mental shortcuts that sometimes lead us astray.

Level 1 · Short introduction

Thinking is using the information we have to draw conclusions, solve problems and make decisions. Some of that thinking is slow and deliberate; much of it is fast and intuitive. Mental shortcuts let us decide without exhausting ourselves, but they also produce systematic errors that can be understood and, in part, corrected.

Level 2 · Fuller explanation

Two ways of thinking

Many researchers distinguish fast thinking, automatic and effortless, from slow thinking, deliberate and costly. The first recognises a face or completes "bread and...". The second works out 17 × 24. Daniel Kahneman popularised them as "System 1" and "System 2", though this is a useful simplification rather than two real parts of the brain.

Shortcuts and biases

  • Availability: we judge as more likely what comes easily to mind; after news of a plane crash, flying seems more dangerous.
  • Representativeness: we judge by resemblance to a stereotype and ignore how many cases there really are.
  • Anchoring: an initial number, even an arbitrary one, influences our estimates.
  • Confirmation bias: we mainly look for and remember what confirms what we already believe.

Solving problems

Solving a problem requires representing it well. Sometimes the solution arrives suddenly, as an insight, after we stop thinking about it. At other times we are blocked by functional fixedness: we fail to think of using an object for something other than its usual purpose.

Thinking better

It helps to consider the opposite possibility, look for data on how often things really happen, use checklists for important decisions and talk decisions through with other people.

Level 3 · Going further, with references

Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman's heuristics and biases programme, from 1974, transformed psychology and economics; Kahneman received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002. Gerd Gigerenzer replied that many heuristics are "fast and frugal" and work very well in real environments, and that some errors disappear when information is presented as frequencies rather than probabilities.

In logical reasoning, the Wason selection task (1966) showed that most people fail an abstract rule but succeed when the problem is about social rules, such as checking the age of someone drinking alcohol. Allen Newell and Herbert Simon (1972) described problem solving as search through a state space, the basis of classical artificial intelligence. Simon coined the idea of bounded rationality.

Hugo Mercier and Dan Sperber proposed that reasoning evolved mainly to argue and persuade others, which would explain why we reason better in groups than alone.

Open debates: whether the two-system model is adequate; why some famous effects, such as "ego depletion", have not replicated; and how emotions and identity influence what we believe.

References

  1. Tversky, A. y Kahneman, D. (1974). Judgment under uncertainty: Heuristics and biases. Science, 185(4157), 1124–1131.
  2. Kahneman, D. (2011). Thinking, Fast and Slow. Nueva York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux.
  3. Gigerenzer, G. y Goldstein, D. G. (1996). Reasoning the fast and frugal way. Psychological Review, 103(4), 650–669.
  4. Mercier, H. y Sperber, D. (2011). Why do humans reason? Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 34(2), 57–74.
